summary:
Ereia helps farmers choose safer, more resilient crops and rotations using NASA Earth data. Built for the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge, it turns satellite and reanalysis data into plain-language guidance on soil water, climate risk, and soil health. It is first calibrated for Argentina's Pampas, our country's agricultural heartland, and built on global datasets to scale.

Growers draw a field on a map. Ereia combines NASA POWER soil moisture, rainfall, evapotranspiration and temperature data with NASA SRTM terrain, ISRIC SoilGrids soil properties, and the NOAA ENSO phase. It does not invent long-range forecasts. Instead, it flags droughts, erosion, and heat or frost risks already underway. For each crop, it estimates a yield range against the local normal and the chance of a bad year. To do this, a model trained on real Argentine yields is run across past years with the same ENSO phase. A rotation matrix then scores soil health. Risk updates weekly during the season.

By showing clear, honest uncertainty, Ereia helps growers protect soil carbon, use stored water wisely, and adapt to climate volatility.
details:
GITHUB
What does it do and how does it work?

Ereia is a farmer-centered decision-support web app for the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge. It is first calibrated for Argentina's Pampas, our country's agricultural heartland, and built on global open datasets so it can scale. It helps growers understand their field's current condition, compare crop options for the active planting season, and protect long-term soil health.

Map your field. Growers draw or select a field on a satellite map. Ereia automatically adds terrain and soil properties to it.

Read current conditions, not fake forecasts. Ereia pulls daily agroclimatic data from NASA POWER: MERRA-2-based root-zone and surface soil wetness, evapotranspiration, bias-corrected precipitation, and temperature extremes. It combines this with NASA SRTM 30 m slope and ISRIC SoilGrids texture and organic carbon. Satellite and reanalysis data describe the present and the past, not the rainfall of the coming months, so Ereia does not invent long-range forecasts. Instead, it flags physical anomalies that are already underway:

  • flash-drought onset
  • "false recharge" (wet topsoil over a dry root zone)
  • runoff and erosion risk on sloped bare soil
  • waterlogging
  • heat and frost exposure

What Ereia predicts. For each candidate crop, Ereia estimates how this season's yield is likely to compare with the long-term trend yield of the field's department. It reports two things:

  • a P10–P90 yield range in qq/ha relative to that trend
  • the probability of a bad year, defined as at least 15% below trend

Soil health is not predicted. It is scored with explicit agronomic rules.

Compare crops with two transparent pillars.

  • Water & climate: a gradient-boosting model trained on real department-level yields from Argentina's Ministry of Agriculture (MAGyP), covering 170 departments. Each yield is measured against that department's long-term trend and adjusted for drought-driven crop abandonment. The model trains on 16 seasons and holds out 3 for testing, including the 2022/23 drought. The coming season's weather is unknown, so the model is run across past years with the same ENSO phase (NOAA ONI, 1981–2025). This gives a distribution of outcomes instead of a single guess. Cover crops (vetch, oats) and camelina have no yield records, so they are scored with FAO-56 yield-response factors.
  • Soil & rotation: an agronomic matrix that scores each crop transition across 11 crops. It accounts for nitrogen fixation, carbon and residue, pest-cycle breaks, months of bare soil, and erosion on slopes. It penalizes monoculture and respects double-crop timing.

Farmers set their priority (water resilience, balanced, or soil conservation) and can test "What-If" soil-moisture and rainfall scenarios.

Follow the season. After sowing, Ereia updates risk every week as observed weather replaces the analog years. Growers can record their harvest and review 20 years of rainfall, soil moisture, and regional yield history.

What benefits does it have?

  • Plain language: "water in the roots," "3 out of 10 seasons end well below your area's normal," "yield vs. your area's normal," with technical detail available on demand.
  • Honest uncertainty: P10–P90 ranges instead of single numbers, visible warnings when an approximate regional value replaces field-level data, and reminders that local agronomic judgment comes first.
  • Reliable: caching, rate limiters, and automatic fallbacks keep it responsive even when external soil or elevation services throttle requests.

What is the intended impact?

La Niña droughts such as Argentina's 2022/23 season, together with erosion on bare soil, threaten both farm income and soil carbon. Ereia turns NASA Earth observations into everyday planning decisions. It helps growers:

  • avoid planting water-hungry crops into depleted soil profiles
  • make better use of the water already stored in the soil
  • adopt cover crops and nitrogen-fixing rotations

Its architecture is built to expand from the rainfed Pampas to other regions of Argentina and the world.

How is the project creative?

  • Analog years instead of fake forecasts. Ereia combines observed soil-moisture memory with what actually happened, at that location, in past years of the same ENSO phase. Uncertainty becomes a risk distribution a farmer can read.
  • Honest about what can be predicted, and built to improve. Before sowing, the coming season's weather is unknown, and we measure exactly how much that limits us. Our expected-yield score is about 3% more accurate than assuming a "normal year," and we say so openly. We put the model to work where it already adds value:
    • Bad-year detection: out of sample across all 19 seasons, it ranks bad years with an AUC of 0.61 at sowing. On the 3 held-out test seasons, which include the 2022/23 drought, it reaches 0.78, against 0.52 for the "normal year" baseline.
    • Calibrated ranges: the P10 and P90 bounds are exceeded 10.8% and 10.3% of the time, against a 10% target.
    • Per-crop honesty gate: a calibrated bad-year probability is shown only where it beats the historical frequency (early and late maize, first- and second-crop soybean). For other crops, the app shows the typical historical frequency.
    • Skill grows during the season: as observed weather replaces analog years, bad-year AUC rises from 0.61 at sowing to 0.70 at season end. Calibrated probabilities also extend from 4 to 7 crops. This is why in-season tracking is a core part of the product.
  • A field-notebook interface instead of a dense GIS dashboard, with consistent color meaning: blue for water, terracotta for heat and soil, green for crops and actions.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Harmonizing scales: combining NASA POWER grid cells of about 50 km, SoilGrids at 250 m, and SRTM at 30 m, while handling NASA POWER's few-day processing lag.
  • Avoiding data leakage: cross-validation grouped by whole seasons, only ENSO values already published at decision time, and historical yields adjusted for drought-driven crop abandonment.
  • Agronomic realism: planting windows, double-crop field occupancy, crop water demand vs. residue cover, and explicit points where local experts must validate results.

Current limits, and how we plan to push them:

  • Resolution: yields are recorded per department and climate cells are about 50 km wide, so neighboring fields can look alike. Harvest records from growers, yield-monitor data, and field sensors will move the model from regional to field level.
  • Extreme droughts: in 2022/23 the bad-year signal at sowing rose above normal (31% vs. 24% typical), but it was still too low and the expected score stayed too optimistic. This is the clearest target for the next version. Adding higher-resolution satellite soil moisture and vegetation indices should help capture droughts earlier.
  • Wide ranges: P10–P90 spans average about ±30% of trend yield. They are honest today, and they should narrow as more seasons, field-level labels, and in-season observations are added.
  • ENSO as the only seasonal signal: analog years capture part of the climate variability, not all of it. Other ocean and climate indices, and seasonal forecast ensembles, are natural next inputs.
  • Expert-based components: cover crops and camelina use FAO parameters, and the rotation matrix encodes agronomic knowledge. Both are transparent and editable, and are ready to be validated with field trials and local agronomists.
  • Data availability: when SoilGrids or elevation services are unavailable, Ereia falls back to regional reference values and tells the user. A full precomputed national layer would remove this dependency.

What's next? (Future roadmap)

  • Field-level learning: use growers' recorded harvests to recalibrate the model locally every season, so the tool gets better the more it is used.
  • Fusing NASA data with growers' own sensors: let farmers connect soil-moisture probes, weather stations, and irrigation logs. Climate cells of about 50 km cannot see farm-level irrigation pulses. Combining ground measurements with NASA climate and terrain baselines will close that gap and enable site-specific irrigation and frost decision support.
  • Higher-resolution Earth observation: integrate SMAP soil moisture, vegetation indices, and new missions such as NISAR to sharpen early drought and crop-stress detection.
  • Expanding across Argentina and irrigated agriculture: extend coverage beyond the Pampas to regional economies, including irrigated valleys and fruit orchards, where crop calendars, frost risk, and water management differ sharply from rainfed grain farming.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Leaflet / react-leaflet (Esri World Imagery base map), deployed on Vercel.
  • Backend & ML: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, httpx, scikit-learn (HistGradientBoostingRegressor), pandas, NumPy, joblib, pytest, deployed on Render.
  • Database & auth: Supabase (PostgreSQL, Auth with Row Level Security, persistent cache).
  • Data: NASA POWER (MERRA-2-based soil wetness, evapotranspiration and bias-corrected precipitation); NASA SRTM 30 m (via OpenTopoData); ISRIC SoilGrids v2; NOAA CPC ONI; FAO-56 / GAEZ v4 parameters; MAGyP crop estimates; Georef AR and Photon geocoding.
  • Hardware: standard laptops. Training and inference run on CPU, at about 5 ms p95 per field.
